content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has published consolidated guidelines on the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis (TB). These guidelines are available under the ISBN 978-92-4-155052-9 and were released in 2019. The suggested citation for this document is: WHO consolidated guidelines on drug-resistant tuberculosis treatment. Geneva: World Health Organization; 2019. The guidelines include detailed recommendations and remarks on various aspects of drug-resistant TB treatment, such as regimens for isoniazid-resistant TB, the composition and duration of longer multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) regimens, the use of standardized shorter MDR-TB regimens, monitoring patient response using culture, initiation of antiretroviral therapy in patients on second-line anti-TB regimens, surgical interventions, and care and support for patients with MDR/RR-TB. Research priorities, acknowledgments, references, and annexes with additional data and methods are also provided. The guidelines have been updated following processes conducted between 2011 and 2018, in accordance with WHO requirements. They replace previous WHO recommendations on the treatment of MDR/RR-TB issued since 2011. The document includes PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcomes) questions, revised dosages for second-line medicines, and key references. The WHO has taken all reasonable precautions to verify the information in this publication. However, the material is distributed without warranty, and the responsibility for its interpretation and use lies with the reader. WHO is not liable for any damages arising from its use. Key definitions in the guidelines include: Drug-susceptibility testing (DST): In vitro testing using phenotypic methods or molecular techniques to detect resistance-conferring mutations. Severe disease: Defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on chest radiography or smear positivity in patients older than 14 years. In children under 15, severe disease includes extrapulmonary forms other than lymphadenopathy. Intensive phase: The initial part of a regimen for MDR/RR-TB treatment, involving injectable agents such as amikacin, capreomycin, kanamycin, or streptomycin. Isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB): Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains resistant to isoniazid but susceptible to rifampicin. Longer MDR-TB regimens: Treatment regimens lasting 18 months or more, which may be standardized or individualized. Shorter MDR-TB regimens: Standardized treatment courses lasting 9–12 months, based on documented evidence. The guidelines also address the management of serious adverse events (SAEs), which may require the termination of the suspected drug. SAEs are defined as adverse events leading to death, life-threatening experiences, prolonged hospitalization, significant disability, or congenital anomalies. The WHO has developed these guidelines using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach, ensuring evidence-based policy recommendations. The development process involved multidisciplinary groups of external experts and affected individuals, overseen by WHO’s Guideline Review Committee (GRC). The guidelines aim to support health professionals in improving the treatment and care of patients with drug-resistant TB, aligning with the goals of the End TB Strategy.
